"abc123..." } } ] } } ``` ## Error Handling ### Falco Runtime Monitor Error Handling **eBPF Driver Load Failures**: - **Scenario**: eBPF driver fails to load due to kernel version incompatibility or missing kernel headers - **Detection**: Falco pod CrashLoopBackOff with error message in logs - **Handling**: - Falco Helm chart includes fallback to kernel module driver - If both fail, alert to Slack with instructions to check kernel version compatibility - Document minimum kernel version requirements (4.14+) in README - **Recovery**: Manual intervention required to upgrade kernel or use compatible driver **Alertmanager Connectivity Failures**: - **Scenario**: Falco cannot reach Alertmanager endpoint - **Detection**: Falco logs show HTTP connection errors - **Handling**: - Falco buffers alerts in memory (up to 1000 alerts) - Retry with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, max 30s) - After 5 minutes of failures, log error and drop oldest alerts - **Recovery**: Automatic reconnection when Alertmanager becomes available **Rule Syntax Errors**: - **Scenario**: Custom Falco rule has invalid syntax - **Detection**: Falco fails to start with rule parsing error in logs - **Handling**: - Validate rules with `falco --validate` in CI/CD pipeline before deployment - Use Helm pre-install hook to validate rules - If validation fails, prevent deployment and surface error to user - **Recovery**: Fix rule syntax and redeploy **High Alert Volume**: - **Scenario**: Falco generates excessive alerts (>100/minute) due to noisy rule or legitimate spike - **Detection**: Prometheus metric `falco_alerts_total` rate exceeds threshold - **Handling**: - Alertmanager groups alerts by rule name with 5-minute window - Alertmanager throttles notifications (max 1 per rule per 15 minutes) - Grafana dashboard shows alert rate trends - **Recovery**: Tune rule conditions to reduce false positives or add exclusions ### Kyverno Supply Chain Verifier Error Handling **Signature Verification Timeout**: - **Scenario**: Cosign verification takes >30 seconds due to Rekor transparency log latency - **Detection**: Kyverno webhook timeout, Pod admission fails with timeout error - **Handling**: - Configure `webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30` in ClusterPolicy - If timeout occurs, Kyverno fails open (admits Pod) and logs warning - Alert to Slack for investigation - **Recovery**: Automatic retry on next Pod creation attempt **Rekor Transparency Log Unavailable**: - **Scenario**: Sigstore Rekor service is down or unreachable - **Detection**: Cosign verification fails with network error - **Handling**: - Kyverno policy includes `failurePolicy: Ignore` for Rekor checks - Verification falls back to certificate-only validation (no transparency log check) - Alert to Slack indicating degraded verification - **Recovery**: Automatic recovery when Rekor becomes available **Certificate Validation Failures**: - **Scenario**: Image signed with certificate that doesn't match expected identity - **Detection**: Kyverno rejects Pod with error message - **Handling**: - In enforce mode: Reject Pod with descriptive error including expected vs actual certificate subject - In audit mode: Log violation to PolicyReport and admit Pod - Error message includes link to documentation on proper signing procedure - **Recovery**: Re-sign image with correct certificate or update policy to accept certificate **Missing Attestations**: - **Scenario**: Image has signature but missing SBOM or SLSA provenance attestation - **Detection**: Kyverno rejects Pod with error message - **Handling**: - In enforce mode: Reject Pod with error specifying which attestation is missing - In audit mode: Log violation to PolicyReport and admit Pod - Error message includes link to CI/CD documentation on generating attestations - **Recovery**: Re-build image with required attestations or temporarily switch namespace to audit mode **Policy Conflict**: - **Scenario**: Multiple Kyverno policies apply to same resource with conflicting requirements - **Detection**: Kyverno logs warning about policy conflict - **Handling**: - Kyverno applies all policies; Pod must satisfy all requirements - If any policy fails, Pod is rejected with combined error message - Use `kubectl describe clusterpolicy` to review policy precedence - **Recovery**: Adjust policy match conditions to eliminate overlap or use PolicyException ### Kubernetes Audit Logging Error Handling **Audit Log File Rotation**: - **Scenario**: Audit log file grows too large and needs rotation - **Detection**: Disk space monitoring shows high usage on control plane nodes - **Handling**: - Configure API server with `--audit-log-maxsize=100` (MB) and `--audit-log-maxbackup=10` - Promtail handles log rotation automatically via inotify - Old log files are compressed and retained for 7 days - **Recovery**: Automatic cleanup after retention period **Promtail Loki Connection Failure**: - **Scenario**: Promtail cannot reach Loki endpoint - **Detection**: Promtail logs show HTTP connection errors - **Handling**: - Promtail buffers logs on disk (up to 10GB in `/var/log/promtail-buffer/`) - Retry with exponential backoff - Alert to Slack if buffer exceeds 80% capacity - **Recovery**: Automatic reconnection when Loki becomes available; buffered logs are shipped **Audit Policy Misconfiguration**: - **Scenario**: Audit policy has invalid syntax or references non-existent resources - **Detection**: API server fails to start with audit policy error in logs - **Handling**: - Validate audit policy with `kubectl apply --dry-run=server` before applying to API server - Use admission controller to validate audit policy syntax - If API server fails to start, revert to previous audit policy - **Recovery**: Fix policy syntax and restart API server **High Audit Log Volume**: - **Scenario**: Audit logs exceed expected volume (>10GB/day) due to verbose policy or high API traffic - **Detection**: Loki ingestion rate exceeds threshold, disk space alerts - **Handling**: - Audit policy excludes high-volume read operations (get, list, watch on ConfigMaps/Secrets) - Promtail drops debug-level audit events in production namespaces - Alert to Slack with recommendation to tune audit policy - **Recovery**: Adjust audit policy to reduce verbosity or increase Loki storage capacity ### CIS Benchmark Compliance Scanner Error Handling **kube-bench Job Failure**: - **Scenario**: kube-bench Job fails due to insufficient permissions or missing host paths - **Detection**: Job status shows Failed, pod logs show permission denied errors - **Handling**: - Job requires privileged security context and host filesystem access - Validate RBAC permissions before running Job - If Job fails, alert to Slack with error message and link to troubleshooting guide - **Recovery**: Fix permissions and manually trigger Job **Scan Result Storage Failure**: - **Scenario**: ConfigMap creation fails due to size limit (1MB) or API server unavailability - **Detection**: kube-bench pod logs show ConfigMap creation error - **Handling**: - If results exceed 1MB, compress JSON and store as gzip - If API server unavailable, retry with exponential backoff (max 5 attempts) - If all retries fail, log results to stdout for manual collection - **Recovery**: Automatic retry on next scheduled scan **Comparison with Previous Scan Failure**: - **Scenario**: Cannot retrieve previous scan results for comparison - **Detection**: kube-bench logs show ConfigMap not found error - **Handling**: - If no previous scan exists, skip comparison and store current results - If previous scan ConfigMap is corrupted, log warning and proceed with current scan - Alert includes note that comparison was skipped - **Recovery**: Automatic recovery on next scan when valid previous results exist **Alert Delivery Failure**: - **Scenario**: kube-bench cannot send alert to Alertmanager - **Detection**: kube-bench pod logs show HTTP connection error - **Handling**: - Retry alert delivery 3 times with 10-second delay - If all retries fail, log error and exit (scan results still stored in ConfigMap) - Grafana dashboard shows scan completion status - **Recovery**: Manual review of scan results in ConfigMap ### Incident Response Runbook Error Handling **Runbook Link Broken**: - **Scenario**: Alert includes link to runbook that returns 404 - **Detection**: User clicks link and receives 404 error - **Handling**: - Maintain runbook index in `secops/runbooks/README.md` with all valid links - Use CI/CD link checker to validate runbook links before merge - If link is broken, alert includes fallback link to runbook index - **Recovery**: Fix broken link in alert configuration and redeploy **Runbook Outdated**: - **Scenario**: Runbook references tools or procedures that no longer exist - **Detection**: User follows runbook and encounters errors - **Handling**: - Include "Last Updated" date at top of each runbook - Review runbooks quarterly and update as needed - Encourage users to submit issues for outdated runbooks - **Recovery**: Update runbook with current procedures **Forensic Evidence Collection Failure**: - **Scenario**: Runbook instructs to collect logs, but logs have been rotated or deleted - **Detection**: User attempts to query logs in Loki and receives no results - **Handling**: - Runbook includes note about log retention period (30 days) - If logs are outside retention window, runbook provides alternative evidence sources - Recommend increasing retention period for critical namespaces - **Recovery**: Adjust log retention policy to prevent future data loss ## Testing Strategy ### Overview The SecOps feature is primarily composed of declarative Infrastructure as Code (IaC) configurations, policy definitions, and documentation. Property-based testing is **not applicable** for this feature because: 1. **Declarative Configuration**: The feature consists of Kubernetes manifests, Helm values, and policy definitions rather than imperative code with testable logic 2. **External Tool Integration**: The core functionality is provided by external tools (Falco, Kyverno, kube-bench) that we configure but do not implement 3. **No Pure Functions**: There are no pure functions with clear input/output behavior that would benefit from property-based testing Instead, the testing strategy focuses on: - **Configuration validation** - Ensuring YAML/JSON syntax is correct and schemas are valid - **Integration testing** - Verifying components work together correctly in a test cluster - **Policy compliance testing** - Validating that policies enforce expected behavior - **Documentation testing** - Ensuring runbooks are accurate and links are valid ### Test Categories #### 1. Configuration Validation Tests **Purpose**: Validate syntax and schema correctness of configuration files before deployment. **Tools**: - `yamllint` for YAML syntax validation - `kubeval` for Kubernetes manifest schema validation - `helm lint` for Helm chart validation - `falco --validate` for Falco rule validation **Test Cases**: ```bash # Validate Falco Helm values helm lint secops/runtime/falco/ # Validate Falco custom rules docker run -v $(pwd)/secops/runtime/falco/rules:/rules \ falcosecurity/falco:latest \ falco --validate /rules/custom-rules.yaml # Validate Kyverno policies kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f secops/supply-chain/ # Validate audit policy kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f secops/runtime/audit-logging/audit-policy.yaml # Validate kube-bench Job kubeval secops/compliance/kube-bench-job.yaml ``` **Automation**: Run in CI/CD pipeline on every pull request using pre-commit hooks and GitHub Actions. #### 2. Integration Tests **Purpose**: Verify components work together correctly in a test Kubernetes cluster. **Environment**: - Kind (Kubernetes in Docker) cluster for local testing - Staging cluster for pre-production validation **Test Scenarios**: **Falco Runtime Detection**: ```bash # Test 1: Verify Falco detects shell spawning kubectl run test-shell --image=nginx --restart=Never -- /bin/bash -c "sleep 10" # Expected: Falco alert "Terminal shell in container" sent to Alertmanager within 5 seconds # Test 2: Verify Falco detects privilege escalation kubectl run test-privesc --image=nginx --restart=Never --privileged -- /bin/bash -c "capsh --print" # Expected: Falco alert "Privilege escalation attempt" sent to Alertmanager # Test 3: Verify Falco alert routing # Expected: Critical alerts appear in PagerDuty, medium alerts in Slack ``` **Kyverno Supply Chain Verification**: ```bash # Test 1: Verify unsigned image is rejected kubectl run test-unsigned --image=nginx:latest --namespace=production # Expected: Admission denied with error "image signature verification failed" # Test 2: Verify signed image is admitted kubectl run test-signed --image=ghcr.io/org/signed-app:v1.0.0 --namespace=production # Expected: Pod created successfully # Test 3: Verify audit mode allows unsigned images kubectl run test-audit --image=nginx:latest --namespace=development # Expected: Pod created, PolicyReport shows failure # Test 4: Verify namespace exclusion kubectl run test-excluded --image=nginx:latest --namespace=kube-system # Expected: Pod created without verification ``` **Audit Logging**: ```bash # Test 1: Verify audit logs are shipped to Loki kubectl create secret generic test-secret --from-literal=key=value --namespace=default sleep 30 # Query Loki: {source="k8s-audit",verb="create",resource="secrets",namespace="default"} # Expected: Audit event appears in Loki within 30 seconds # Test 2: Verify sensitive data is excluded # Expected: Audit log shows metadata level (no secret value in log) # Test 3: Verify authentication failures are logged kubectl get pods --as=unauthorized-user # Expected: Audit event with verb="get", user="unauthorized-user", response_code="403" ``` **CIS Benchmark Scanning**: ```bash # Test 1: Verify kube-bench Job completes successfully kubectl apply -f secops/compliance/kube-bench-job.yaml kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/kube-bench --timeout=5m # Expected: Job completes, ConfigMap created with results # Test 2: Verify scan results are stored kubectl get configmap -l scan-type=cis-benchmark # Expected: ConfigMap exists with JSON results # Test 3: Verify alert on new failures # Manually introduce failure (e.g., disable anonymous-auth) # Run scan again # Expected: Alert sent to Alertmanager with "new failures detected" ``` **Automation**: Run integration tests in CI/CD pipeline using GitHub Actions with Kind cluster. Run nightly in staging cluster. #### 3. Policy Compliance Tests **Purpose**: Validate that Kyverno policies enforce expected security requirements. **Test Framework**: Kyverno CLI `kyverno test` command **Test Cases**: ```yaml # secops/supply-chain/test-cosign-verify.yaml apiVersion: cli.kyverno.io/v1alpha1 kind: Test metadata: name: test-cosign-verify-policy policies: - ../cosign-verify-policy.yaml resources: - test-resources.yaml results: - policy: verify-image-signature rule: verify-signature resource: unsigned-pod kind: Pod result: fail - policy: verify-image-signature rule: verify-signature resource: signed-pod kind: Pod result: pass ``` ```yaml # test-resources.yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: unsigned-pod namespace: production spec: containers: - name: app image: nginx:latest --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: signed-pod namespace: production spec: containers: - name: app image: ghcr.io/org/signed-app:v1.0.0@sha256:abc123 ``` **Run Tests**: ```bash kyverno test secops/supply-chain/ ``` **Automation**: Run in CI/CD pipeline on every pull request. #### 4. Documentation Tests **Purpose**: Ensure runbooks are accurate and all links are valid. **Tools**: - `markdown-link-check` for link validation - Manual review for procedure accuracy **Test Cases**: ```bash # Validate all links in runbooks find secops/runbooks/ -name "*.md" -exec markdown-link-check {} \; # Validate links in README markdown-link-check secops/README.md # Validate control mapping references # Ensure all kube-bench test IDs referenced in control mappings exist grep -r "test_number" secops/compliance/controls/ | \ while read line; do test_id=$(echo $line | grep -oP 'test_number: \K[0-9.]+') # Verify test_id exists in kube-bench output done ``` **Automation**: Run link checker in CI/CD pipeline on every pull request. #### 5. End-to-End Scenario Tests **Purpose**: Validate complete incident response workflows. **Test Scenarios**: **Scenario 1: Compromised Pod Detection and Response** 1. Deploy pod with known malicious behavior (spawn shell, read /etc/shadow) 2. Verify Falco detects behavior and sends alert to Alertmanager 3. Verify alert is routed to PagerDuty 4. Follow compromised-pod.md runbook to: - Identify pod from alert - Capture forensic evidence (logs, process list) - Query audit logs in Loki for pod creation event - Isolate pod with NetworkPolicy - Terminate pod 5. Verify all steps complete successfully **Scenario 2: Unsigned Image Deployment Attempt** 1. Attempt to deploy unsigned image to production namespace 2. Verify Kyverno rejects deployment with descriptive error 3. Verify PolicyReport shows failure 4. Follow supply-chain-incident.md runbook to: - Identify image from PolicyReport - Query audit logs for who attempted deployment - Scan image for malware - Verify image provenance 5. Verify all steps complete successfully **Scenario 3: CIS Benchmark Failure Remediation** 1. Run kube-bench scan 2. Identify failing control (e.g., anonymous-auth enabled) 3. Follow cis-kubernetes.md control mapping to find remediation 4. Apply remediation (disable anonymous-auth) 5. Re-run scan 6. Verify control now passes **Automation**: Run end-to-end tests weekly in staging cluster. Document results in test report. ### Test Execution Schedule | Test Category | Frequency | Environment | Trigger | |---------------|-----------|-------------|---------| | Configuration Validation | Every PR | CI/CD | Pull request | | Policy Compliance Tests | Every PR | CI/CD | Pull request | | Documentation Tests | Every PR | CI/CD | Pull request | | Integration Tests (Falco) | Daily | Kind cluster | Scheduled | | Integration Tests (Kyverno) | Daily | Kind cluster | Scheduled | | Integration Tests (Audit) | Daily | Kind cluster | Scheduled | | Integration Tests (kube-bench) | Weekly | Staging cluster | Scheduled | | End-to-End Scenarios | Weekly | Staging cluster | Scheduled | | Manual Runbook Review | Quarterly | N/A | Manual | ### Test Coverage Goals - **Configuration Files**: 100% validated for syntax and schema correctness - **Kyverno Policies**: 100% covered by policy compliance tests - **Falco Rules**: 80% covered by integration tests (some rules require specific conditions) - **Runbooks**: 100% link validation, 80% procedure validation via E2E tests - **Integration Points**: 100% covered (Alertmanager, Loki, Slack, PagerDuty) ### Continuous Improvement - **Test Failure Analysis**: Review all test failures in weekly security meeting - **Runbook Updates**: Update runbooks based on actual incident response experiences - **Policy Tuning**: Adjust Falco rules and Kyverno policies based on false positive rates - **Coverage Expansion**: Add new test cases when new features are added or bugs are discovered

# Requirements Document

## Introduction

The SecOps feature provides operational security workflows and runtime controls for Kubernetes environments. This feature complements the existing shift-left security scanning in the security/ folder by adding runtime threat detection, compliance auditing, supply chain verification at admission time, and incident response runbooks. The feature integrates with existing observability (Loki, Prometheus) and notification (Slack, PagerDuty) infrastructure.

## Glossary

- **Falco**: Runtime security monitoring tool that detects anomalous behavior in containers and Kubernetes
- **Kyverno**: Kubernetes policy engine for admission control and validation
- **Cosign**: Tool for signing and verifying container images using Sigstore
- **SBOM**: Software Bill of Materials - inventory of software components
- **SLSA**: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts - framework for supply chain integrity
- **CIS_Benchmark**: Center for Internet Security Kubernetes security configuration benchmark
- **Kube_Bench**: Tool that checks Kubernetes clusters against CIS Benchmark
- **Audit_Log**: Kubernetes API server audit log recording all API requests
- **Loki**: Log aggregation system (existing in observability/loki/)
- **Alertmanager**: Alert routing and notification system (part of Prometheus stack)
- **Admission_Controller**: Kubernetes component that intercepts API requests before persistence
- **Rekor**: Sigstore transparency log for signature verification
- **Attestation**: Cryptographically signed metadata about an artifact
- **Provenance**: Record of how an artifact was built (SLSA provenance)
- **SecOps_System**: The complete operational security system defined in this specification
- **Runtime_Monitor**: Falco-based runtime security monitoring subsystem
- **Compliance_Scanner**: Kube-bench-based compliance scanning subsystem
- **Supply_Chain_Verifier**: Kyverno-based supply chain verification subsystem
- **Incident_Responder**: Human operator following incident response runbooks

## Requirements

### Requirement 1: Runtime Threat Detection

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want to detect suspicious runtime behavior in containers, so that I can identify and respond to potential security incidents.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. WHEN a container spawns an unexpected shell (bash, sh, zsh) in a production namespace, THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL generate a high-severity alert
2. WHEN a process attempts privilege escalation (setuid, setgid, capabilities modification), THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL generate a critical-severity alert
3. WHEN a container makes an unexpected outbound network connection to an IP address not in the allowlist, THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL generate a medium-severity alert
4. WHEN a sensitive file is accessed (e.g., /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, private keys), THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL generate a high-severity alert
5. THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL use Falco rules defined in secops/runtime/falco/rules/custom-rules.yaml
6. THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL route alerts to Alertmanager using the configuration in secops/runtime/falco/rules/alerts.yaml
7. WHEN Falco is deployed, THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL use Helm values from secops/runtime/falco/values.yaml

### Requirement 2: Alert Integration

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want runtime security alerts routed to existing notification channels, so that I receive timely notifications without managing separate alerting infrastructure.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. WHEN the Runtime_Monitor generates an alert, THE Runtime_Monitor SHALL send the alert to Alertmanager
2. WHEN Alertmanager receives a security alert, THE Alertmanager SHALL route critical and high-severity alerts to PagerDuty using the configuration in notifications/pagerduty-notify.yml
3. WHEN Alertmanager receives a security alert, THE Alertmanager SHALL route medium-severity alerts to Slack using the configuration in notifications/slack-notify.yml
4. THE alert payload SHALL include the pod name, namespace, rule name, severity, and timestamp
5. THE alert payload SHALL include a link to the relevant incident response runbook in secops/runbooks/

### Requirement 3: Kubernetes Audit Logging

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want Kubernetes API audit logs shipped to Loki, so that I can investigate security incidents and maintain compliance audit trails.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL define a Kubernetes audit policy in secops/runtime/audit-logging/audit-policy.yaml
2. THE audit policy SHALL log all create, update, delete, and patch operations at RequestResponse level
3. THE audit policy SHALL log authentication and authorization failures at Metadata level
4. THE audit policy SHALL exclude read operations on ConfigMaps and Secrets to reduce log volume
5. WHEN the audit policy is applied to the Kubernetes API server, THE API server SHALL generate audit log entries for matching requests
6. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a log shipper configuration in secops/runtime/audit-logging/loki-shipper.yaml
7. WHEN the log shipper is deployed, THE log shipper SHALL send audit logs to the Loki instance defined in observability/loki/values.yaml
8. THE log shipper SHALL add labels for cluster name, environment, and log source to enable filtering in Grafana

### Requirement 4: Supply Chain Verification at Admission

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want to enforce that only signed container images with valid SBOM attestations are deployed, so that I prevent supply chain attacks.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL define a Kyverno policy in secops/supply-chain/cosign-verify-policy.yaml
2. WHEN a Pod creation or update request is received, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the container image signature using cosign
3. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify signatures against the Sigstore Rekor transparency log
4. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the certificate identity matches the expected GitHub Actions workflow URL pattern
5. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the certificate OIDC issuer is https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
6. WHEN signature verification fails, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL reject the Pod creation request with a descriptive error message
7. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/supply-chain=audit`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL log verification failures without blocking deployment

### Requirement 5: SBOM Attestation Verification

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want to enforce that container images have valid SBOM attestations, so that I maintain visibility into software components in production.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL define a Kyverno policy in secops/supply-chain/sbom-policy.yaml
2. WHEN a Pod creation or update request is received, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify an SBOM attestation exists for the container image
3. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the SBOM attestation is in SPDX-JSON format
4. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the SBOM attestation is signed and attached as an OCI referrer
5. WHEN SBOM verification fails, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL reject the Pod creation request with a descriptive error message
6. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/sbom=audit`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL log verification failures without blocking deployment

### Requirement 6: SLSA Provenance Verification

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want to verify SLSA provenance attestations for container images, so that I ensure images were built by trusted CI/CD pipelines.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL define a Kyverno policy in secops/supply-chain/slsa-verify.yaml
2. WHEN a Pod creation or update request is received, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify a SLSA provenance attestation exists for the container image
3. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the provenance builder identity matches the expected GitHub Actions workflow
4. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the provenance includes the git repository and commit SHA
5. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL verify the provenance is signed using the GitHub OIDC token
6. WHEN provenance verification fails, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL reject the Pod creation request with a descriptive error message
7. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/slsa=audit`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL log verification failures without blocking deployment

### Requirement 7: CIS Benchmark Compliance Scanning

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want to scan Kubernetes clusters against CIS Benchmark, so that I identify and remediate security misconfigurations.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL define a Kubernetes Job in secops/compliance/kube-bench-job.yaml
2. WHEN the Job is executed, THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL run kube-bench against the cluster
3. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL scan control plane components (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd)
4. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL scan worker node configurations
5. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL output results in JSON format
6. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL store results as a ConfigMap with timestamp and cluster labels
7. WHEN the scan completes, THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL send a summary to Slack using notifications/slack-notify.yml

### Requirement 8: Scheduled Compliance Scanning

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want automated weekly CIS Benchmark scans, so that I maintain continuous compliance visibility.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL define a Kubernetes CronJob in secops/compliance/kube-bench-cronjob.yaml
2. THE CronJob SHALL execute the kube-bench Job every Sunday at 02:00 UTC
3. THE CronJob SHALL retain the last 3 scan results
4. WHEN a scheduled scan detects new failures compared to the previous scan, THE Compliance_Scanner SHALL generate a high-severity alert to Alertmanager

### Requirement 9: Compliance Control Mapping

**User Story:** As a compliance auditor, I want documentation mapping CIS Benchmark controls to SOC2 and ISO 27001 requirements, so that I can demonstrate compliance coverage.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a CIS Kubernetes control mapping in secops/compliance/controls/cis-kubernetes.md
2. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a SOC2 control mapping in secops/compliance/controls/soc2.md
3. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide an ISO 27001 control mapping in secops/compliance/controls/iso27001.md
4. THE control mapping documents SHALL reference specific kube-bench test IDs
5. THE control mapping documents SHALL reference corresponding Kyverno policies in policy/kyverno/ and secops/supply-chain/
6. THE control mapping documents SHALL reference audit log requirements in secops/runtime/audit-logging/audit-policy.yaml

### Requirement 10: Compromised Pod Incident Response

**User Story:** As an incident responder, I want a runbook for responding to compromised pods, so that I can preserve evidence and contain the incident effectively.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a runbook in secops/runbooks/compromised-pod.md
2. THE runbook SHALL include steps to identify the compromised pod from Falco alerts
3. THE runbook SHALL include steps to capture forensic evidence (logs, process list, network connections, filesystem snapshot)
4. THE runbook SHALL include steps to preserve audit logs from Loki for the affected namespace and time window
5. THE runbook SHALL include steps to isolate the pod using NetworkPolicy before termination
6. THE runbook SHALL include steps to analyze the container image for malware or backdoors
7. THE runbook SHALL include steps to rotate credentials that may have been exposed
8. THE runbook SHALL include steps to document findings and update detection rules

### Requirement 11: Secret Exposure Incident Response

**User Story:** As an incident responder, I want a runbook for responding to credential leaks, so that I can rotate secrets and assess impact quickly.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a runbook in secops/runbooks/secret-exposure.md
2. THE runbook SHALL include steps to identify which secret was exposed
3. THE runbook SHALL include steps to immediately rotate the exposed credential using security/secret-rotation/ procedures
4. THE runbook SHALL include steps to query audit logs in Loki to identify all API requests using the exposed credential
5. THE runbook SHALL include steps to identify all pods that mounted the exposed secret
6. THE runbook SHALL include steps to assess whether the credential was used for unauthorized access
7. THE runbook SHALL include steps to notify affected stakeholders
8. THE runbook SHALL include steps to update secret detection rules in security/secret-detection/ to prevent recurrence

### Requirement 12: Supply Chain Incident Response

**User Story:** As an incident responder, I want a runbook for responding to unsigned or tampered images, so that I can contain supply chain attacks.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a runbook in secops/runbooks/supply-chain-incident.md
2. THE runbook SHALL include steps to identify the unsigned or tampered image from Kyverno policy violation alerts
3. THE runbook SHALL include steps to verify whether the image was deployed despite policy enforcement
4. THE runbook SHALL include steps to query audit logs to identify who attempted to deploy the image
5. THE runbook SHALL include steps to scan the image for malware using security/container-scanning/ tools
6. THE runbook SHALL include steps to verify the image provenance against expected CI/CD workflows
7. THE runbook SHALL include steps to quarantine the image by adding it to a deny list
8. THE runbook SHALL include steps to investigate the CI/CD pipeline for compromise

### Requirement 13: Node Compromise Incident Response

**User Story:** As an incident responder, I want a runbook for responding to compromised Kubernetes nodes, so that I can safely remove the node while preserving evidence.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a runbook in secops/runbooks/node-compromise.md

### Requirement 18: Audit Policy Configuration

**User Story:** As a security operator, I want a Kubernetes audit policy that balances security visibility with log volume, so that I capture relevant events without overwhelming storage.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide an audit policy in secops/runtime/audit-logging/audit-policy.yaml
2. THE audit policy SHALL log authentication failures at Metadata level
3. THE audit policy SHALL log authorization failures at Metadata level
4. THE audit policy SHALL log create, update, delete, patch operations on Secrets at Metadata level (exclude secret values)
5. THE audit policy SHALL log create, update, delete, patch operations on Pods, Deployments, Services at RequestResponse level
6. THE audit policy SHALL log create, update, delete operations on RBAC resources at RequestResponse level
7. THE audit policy SHALL exclude get, list, watch operations on ConfigMaps and Secrets to reduce volume
8. THE audit policy SHALL exclude system component requests (kube-proxy, kube-scheduler) to reduce noise

### Requirement 19: Audit Log Shipper Configuration

**User Story:** As a platform engineer, I want a log shipper configuration for sending audit logs to Loki, so that I can deploy it consistently.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. THE SecOps_System SHALL provide a log shipper configuration in secops/runtime/audit-logging/loki-shipper.yaml
2. THE log shipper SHALL be deployed as a DaemonSet on control plane nodes
3. THE log shipper SHALL read audit logs from the Kubernetes API server log file path
4. THE log shipper SHALL parse audit log JSON format
5. THE log shipper SHALL add labels for cluster name, environment, and log source
6. THE log shipper SHALL send logs to the Loki endpoint defined in observability/loki/values.yaml
7. THE log shipper SHALL buffer logs locally during Loki unavailability
8. THE log shipper SHALL configure resource requests and limits

### Requirement 20: Supply Chain Policy Namespace Exclusions

**User Story:** As a platform engineer, I want to exclude specific namespaces from supply chain verification, so that I can deploy unsigned images in development environments.

#### Acceptance Criteria

1. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/supply-chain=disabled`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL skip signature verification for pods in that namespace
2. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/sbom=disabled`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL skip SBOM verification for pods in that namespace
3. WHERE a namespace has the label `policy.kyverno.io/slsa=disabled`, THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL skip SLSA provenance verification for pods in that namespace
4. THE Supply_Chain_Verifier SHALL log all policy skips with namespace name and reason
5. THE kube-system and kube-public namespaces SHALL be excluded from supply chain verification by default

## Notes

- This feature is entirely configuration-based (YAML, JSON, Markdown) with no traditional programming code
- All components integrate with existing infrastructure: Loki (observability/loki/), Prometheus, Alertmanager, Slack (notifications/slack-notify.yml), PagerDuty (notifications/pagerduty-notify.yml)
- Kyverno policies leverage existing Kyverno installation in `policy/kyverno/`
- Supply chain verification requires images to be signed with Cosign and have SBOM/SLSA attestations
- Namespace labels control policy enforcement modes: enforce (default), audit, or disabled
- Falco uses eBPF driver for better portability across Kubernetes distributions
- Audit logs are shipped to Loki with 30-day retention policy
- CIS Benchmark scans run weekly and alert on new failures
- All runbooks follow consistent structure: Detection → Immediate Actions → Investigation → Remediation → Post-Incident
- Each task references specific requirements for traceability

# Pre-commit is the first local gate before CI.
# Heavy repository-wide hooks such as Checkov and mypy are intentionally excluded from the default pre-push stage
# so final push feedback stays fast; only the lightweight gitleaks secret scan runs at pre-push by default.
minimum_pre_commit_version: '3.7.0'
default_install_hook_types:
  - pre-commit
  - pre-push
default_stages:
  - pre-commit

repos:
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # Secret detection
  # Catch credentials before they ever leave a developer machine.
  # Mirrors the CI gitleaks workflow but runs locally so secrets never leave the machine.
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.18.4
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks
        stages: [pre-push]
        pass_filenames: false

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # IaC quality
  # Keep infrastructure syntax and policy checks close to the edit so broken Terraform, weak policies,
  # and Dockerfile issues are caught before the slower CI security workflows run.
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  - repo: https://github.com/antonbabenko/pre-commit-terraform
    rev: v1.96.3
    hooks:
      - id: terraform_fmt
        files: ^terraform/.*\.tf(vars)?$
      - id: terraform_validate
        files: ^terraform/.*\.tf(vars)?$
        pass_filenames: false

  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: checkov-terraform
        name: checkov (terraform)
        entry: checkov --directory terraform --framework terraform --quiet --compact
        language: python
        additional_dependencies:
          - checkov==3.2.72
        files: ^terraform/.*\.tf(vars)?$
        pass_filenames: false

  - repo: https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint
    rev: v2.12.0
    hooks:
      - id: hadolint
        files: (^|/)([Dd]ockerfile|.*\.Dockerfile)$

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # General code quality
  # These fast text-level checks enforce the repository's EditorConfig-style whitespace, file endings,
  # and structured-data hygiene before language-specific linters spend time on deeper analysis.
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v5.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: check-yaml
        args: [--allow-multiple-documents]
      - id: check-json
      - id: check-merge-conflict
      - id: detect-private-key
      - id: mixed-line-ending
        args: [--fix=lf]

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # Python
  # Reuse the shared pyproject settings for linting, formatting, and type checks so local edits match CI behaviour
  # without forcing developers to remember separate command lines.
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: ruff-check
        name: ruff check
        entry: ruff check --config quality/python/pyproject.toml
        language: python
        additional_dependencies:
          - ruff==0.6.9
        files: \.py$
      - id: ruff-format
        name: ruff format
        entry: ruff format --config quality/python/pyproject.toml
        language: python
        additional_dependencies:
          - ruff==0.6.9
        files: \.py$
      - id: mypy
        name: mypy
        entry: mypy --config-file quality/python/pyproject.toml
        language: python
        additional_dependencies:
          - mypy==1.10.0
        files: \.py$
        pass_filenames: false

  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  # Shell scripts
  # ShellCheck catches quoting, word-splitting, and portability defects early, which matters for the helper scripts
  # in this repository because they are usually executed in automation after only a light manual review.
  # ------------------------------------------------------------
  - repo: https://github.com/shellcheck-py/shellcheck-py
    rev: v0.10.0.1
    hooks:
      - id: shellcheck
        files: \.sh$

variable "project" {}

variable "dr_region" { default = "us-west-2" }                     # <-- CHANGE THIS: secondary region for DR
variable "db_instance_class" { default = "db.t3.medium" }          # <-- CHANGE THIS
variable "db_engine_version" { default = "15.4" }                  # <-- CHANGE THIS: PostgreSQL version
variable "backup_retention_days" { default = 7 }                   # <-- CHANGE THIS: 1–35 days
variable "enable_cross_region_replica" { default = false }         # <-- CHANGE THIS: set true to create DR replica

# ── RDS Instance with PITR ───────────────────────────────────
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier        = "rds-${var.project}-${var.environment}"
  engine            = "postgres"
  engine_version    = var.db_engine_version
  instance_class    = var.db_instance_class
  allocated_storage = 100           # <-- CHANGE THIS (GiB)
  storage_encrypted = true

  # Note 1: backup_retention_period > 0 enables automated backups and
  # point-in-time recovery. PITR allows restore to any second within the
  # retention window. Minimum recommended: 7 days.
  backup_retention_period = var.backup_retention_days

  # Note 2: The backup window should be outside your peak traffic hours.
  # Format: hh24:mi-hh24:mi UTC.
  backup_window      = "02:00-03:00"    # <-- CHANGE THIS
  maintenance_window = "sun:04:00-sun:05:00"  # <-- CHANGE THIS

  # Note 3: Multi-AZ creates a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ.
  # Automatic failover happens in 1-2 minutes if the primary fails.
  # Enable for production workloads.
  multi_az = var.environment == "production" ? true : false

  deletion_protection = var.environment == "production" ? true : false
  skip_final_snapshot = var.environment == "production" ? false : true

  final_snapshot_identifier = var.environment == "production" ? (
    "rds-${var.project}-${var.environment}-final-snapshot"

    Environment = var.environment
  }

# ── Cross-Region Read Replica for DR ─────────────────────────
# Note 4: This creates a read replica in a secondary region. In a DR event,

resource "aws_db_instance" "dr_replica" {
  count    = var.enable_cross_region_replica ? 1 : 0

  identifier             = "rds-${var.project}-${var.environment}-dr"
  replicate_source_db    = aws_db_instance.main.arn
  instance_class         = var.db_instance_class
  backup_retention_period = var.backup_retention_days
  backup_window          = "03:00-04:00"
  storage_encrypted      = true
  skip_final_snapshot    = false
  deletion_protection    = true

  tags = {
    Name        = "rds-${var.project}-${var.environment}-dr"
    Project     = var.project
    Environment = var.environment

}

# ============================================================
# TEMPLATE: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server — Backups
# WHEN TO USE: Add to your existing Terraform module that creates an
#   Azure PostgreSQL Flexible Server. Enables geo-redundant backups
#   and configures a geo-restore replica for DR.
#
# WHAT TO CHANGE: Variables at the top. Integrate into your existing module.
# RELATED FILES: terraform/azure-aks/, terraform/azure-app-service/
# MATURITY: Stable
# ============================================================

variable "project" {}
variable "environment" {}
variable "location" { default = "eastus" }                 # <-- CHANGE THIS: primary region
variable "dr_location" { default = "westus" }              # <-- CHANGE THIS: secondary region for geo-restore
variable "postgres_sku_name" { default = "GP_Standard_D4s_v3" }   # <-- CHANGE THIS
variable "postgres_version" { default = "15" }             # <-- CHANGE THIS
variable "backup_retention_days" { default = 7 }           # <-- CHANGE THIS: 7–35 days
variable "enable_geo_redundant_backup" { default = true }  # <-- CHANGE THIS: required for geo-restore

# ── PostgreSQL Flexible Server with PITR ─────────────────────
resource "azurerm_postgresql_flexible_server" "main" {
  name                = "psql-${var.project}-${var.environment}"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.main.name
  location            = var.location
  version             = var.postgres_version
  sku_name            = var.postgres_sku_name

  # Note 1: geo_redundant_backup_enabled = true replicates backup files to
  # the paired Azure region. This is a prerequisite for geo-restore (RPO ~1h).
  # It cannot be changed after server creation — plan ahead.
  geo_redundant_backup_enabled = var.enable_geo_redundant_backup
  backup_retention_days        = var.backup_retention_days

  # Note 2: zone = "1" combined with standby_availability_zone = "2" enables
  # High Availability with a synchronous hot standby in a different AZ.
  # Automatic failover takes < 120 seconds.
  high_availability {
    mode                      = var.environment == "production" ? "ZoneRedundant" : "Disabled"
    standby_availability_zone = "2"   # <-- CHANGE THIS
  }

  zone = "1"   # <-- CHANGE THIS: primary availability zone

  administrator_login    = "psqladmin"    # <-- CHANGE THIS: admin username
  administrator_password = var.db_admin_password

  storage_mb = 32768   # <-- CHANGE THIS: 32 GiB minimum

  tags = {
    Project     = var.project
    Environment = var.environment
  }
}

# ── Geo-Restore (DR) ─────────────────────────────────────────
# Note 3: Geo-restore creates a new server from the geo-redundant backup
# in the paired region. This is a MANUAL step — it is not automatic.
#
# To perform geo-restore via az CLI (not Terraform — do this during a DR event):
#   az postgres flexible-server geo-restore \
#     --name psql-<project>-<env>-dr \
#     --resource-group <dr-rg> \
#     --location westus \
#     --source-server /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL/flexibleServers/psql-<project>-<env> \
#     --geo-redundant-backup Enabled
#
# Geo-restore RPO: ~1 hour (replication lag to paired region)
# Geo-restore RTO: ~30–60 minutes to provision a new server

# ── Point-in-Time Restore ────────────────────────────────────
# Note 4: To restore to a specific point in time (up to backup_retention_days ago):
#   az postgres flexible-server restore \
#     --name psql-<project>-<env>-restored \
#     --resource-group <rg> \
#     --source-server psql-<project>-<env> \
#     --restore-time "2024-01-15T02:00:00Z"
#
# The restored server is independent — no traffic is automatically redirected.
# Update your connection string after validating the restore.

# ============================================================
# TEMPLATE: GCP Cloud SQL — Backups and Cross-Region Replica
# WHEN TO USE: Add to your existing Terraform module that creates a
#   Cloud SQL instance. Enables automated backups, PITR, and optionally
#   creates a cross-region read replica for DR.
#
# WHAT TO CHANGE: Variables at the top. Integrate into your existing module.
# RELATED FILES: terraform/gcp-gke/
# MATURITY: Stable
# ============================================================

variable "project_id" {}                                # <-- CHANGE THIS: GCP project ID
variable "project" {}
variable "environment" {}
variable "region" { default = "us-central1" }           # <-- CHANGE THIS
variable "dr_region" { default = "us-east1" }           # <-- CHANGE THIS: DR region
variable "db_tier" { default = "db-custom-4-15360" }    # <-- CHANGE THIS: 4 vCPU, 15 GB RAM
variable "postgres_version" { default = "POSTGRES_15" } # <-- CHANGE THIS
variable "backup_start_time" { default = "02:00" }      # <-- CHANGE THIS: HH:MM UTC
variable "backup_retained_backups" { default = 7 }      # <-- CHANGE THIS: 1–365
variable "enable_dr_replica" { default = false }        # <-- CHANGE THIS: set true to create cross-region replica

# ── Cloud SQL Instance with PITR ─────────────────────────────
resource "google_sql_database_instance" "main" {
  name             = "sql-${var.project}-${var.environment}"
  project          = var.project_id
  region           = var.region
  database_version = var.postgres_version

  deletion_protection = var.environment == "production" ? true : false

  settings {
    tier              = var.db_tier
    availability_type = var.environment == "production" ? "REGIONAL" : "ZONAL"  # Note 1: REGIONAL = HA with automatic failover

    backup_configuration {
      enabled    = true
      start_time = var.backup_start_time

      # Note 2: point_in_time_recovery_enabled uses transaction logs to allow
      # restore to any second within the retained_backups * 1-day window.
      # Requires binary logging (PostgreSQL: WAL archiving enabled automatically).
      point_in_time_recovery_enabled = true
      transaction_log_retention_days = 7   # <-- CHANGE THIS

      backup_retention_settings {
        retained_backups = var.backup_retained_backups
        retention_unit   = "COUNT"
      }
    }

    ip_configuration {
      ipv4_enabled    = false   # Note 3: Disable public IP — use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy or Private IP
      private_network = google_compute_network.main.id  # <-- CHANGE THIS: reference your VPC
    }

    maintenance_window {
      day          = 7   # Sunday
      hour         = 4   # 04:00 UTC
      update_track = "stable"
    }

    insights_config {
      query_insights_enabled  = true
      record_application_tags = true
      record_client_address   = false
    }
  }
}

# ── Cross-Region Read Replica for DR ─────────────────────────
# Note 4: Cloud SQL read replicas in a different region serve as the
# DR target. During a DR event, promote the replica:
#   gcloud sql instances promote-replica sql-<project>-<env>-dr --project <project>
# Promotion takes ~5-10 minutes. The replica becomes a standalone primary.
resource "google_sql_database_instance" "dr_replica" {
  count = var.enable_dr_replica ? 1 : 0

  name                 = "sql-${var.project}-${var.environment}-dr"
  project              = var.project_id
  region               = var.dr_region
  database_version     = var.postgres_version
  master_instance_name = google_sql_database_instance.main.name

  deletion_protection = true

  settings {
    tier = var.db_tier

    # Note 5: Read replicas use async replication. Typical lag is < 5 seconds
    # under normal load but can increase during heavy write bursts.
    # Monitor replication lag in Cloud SQL metrics: database/replication/replica_lag.
    backup_configuration {
      enabled = true

      backup_retention_settings {
        retained_backups = var.backup_retained_backups
      }
    }

    ip_configuration {
      ipv4_enabled = false
    }
  }
}

VELERO_NAMESPACE="velero"

  namespace: velero
spec:

#   backup of all namespaces (or a filtered subset) stored in
#   the configured BackupStorageLocation (S3 / Azure Blob / GCS).
#
# WHAT TO CHANGE: Lines marked  # <-- CHANGE THIS
# RELATED FILES: backup/velero/aws-install.sh
#                backup/velero/namespace-backup.yaml
# MATURITY: Stable
# ============================================================

apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: daily-full-backup                     # <-- CHANGE THIS
  namespace: velero
spec:
  # Note 1: Cron syntax — this runs at 02:00 UTC every day.
  # Adjust to a low-traffic window in your time zone.

  template:
    # Note 2: ttl controls how long backups are retained before Velero

      - kube-node-lease

    snapshotVolumes: true

    hooks: {}

  useOwnerReferencesInBackup: false

# ============================================================
# TEMPLATE: cert-manager Bootstrap — ClusterIssuer + Let's Encrypt
# WHEN TO USE: First-time cert-manager setup on any Kubernetes cluster.
#              Provisions TLS certificates automatically via ACME
#              (Let's Encrypt) for all Ingress resources that reference
#              the cluster-issuer annotation.
#
# INSTALL ORDER:
#   Step 1 — Install cert-manager CRDs + controller (once per cluster)
#   Step 2 — Apply this file (ClusterIssuers)
#   Step 3 — Annotate your Ingress (see _base/ingress.yaml) — done
#
# STEP 1 — Install cert-manager via Helm (run once):
#
#   helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
#   helm repo update
#   helm upgrade --install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \
#     --namespace cert-manager --create-namespace \
#     --version v1.14.4 \                          # <-- CHANGE THIS: use latest stable
#     --set crds.enabled=true \
#     --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager \
#     --set prometheus.enabled=true \              # recommended for production
#     --set webhook.timeoutSeconds=30
#
#   # Verify all pods are Running before applying this file:
#   kubectl get pods -n cert-manager
#
# WHAT TO CHANGE: Lines marked  # <-- CHANGE THIS
# RELATED FILES: cd/kubernetes/_base/ingress.yaml
# MATURITY: Stable
# ============================================================

---
# ── 1. Staging ClusterIssuer (use FIRST to avoid rate-limit hits) ─────────
# Let's Encrypt staging has very generous rate limits but produces
# untrusted certificates.  Use it during initial setup and CI testing.
#
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com                 # <-- CHANGE THIS: your ops email
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging-account-key     # stored in cert-manager namespace
    solvers:
      # HTTP-01 challenge: works for any public-facing cluster.
      # For private clusters or wildcard certs, use DNS-01 (see below).
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx             # <-- CHANGE THIS: match your ingress class

---
# ── 2. Production ClusterIssuer ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Only switch to this after staging works — production has strict
# rate limits (50 certs/domain/week).
#
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: platform@example.com                 # <-- CHANGE THIS
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx             # <-- CHANGE THIS

---
# ── 3. DNS-01 ClusterIssuer (for wildcard or private-cluster certs) ───────
# Uncomment and configure one of the DNS provider blocks.
# See https://cert-manager.io/docs/configuration/acme/dns01/
#
# --- Route53 (AWS) ---
# apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
# kind: ClusterIssuer
# metadata:
#   name: letsencrypt-prod-dns
# spec:
#   acme:
#     server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
#     email: platform@example.com
#     privateKeySecretRef:
#       name: letsencrypt-prod-dns-key
#     solvers:
#       - dns01:
#           route53:
#             region: us-east-1               # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             hostedZoneID: ABCDEF1234567     # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             role: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/cert-manager-route53  # <-- CHANGE THIS (IRSA)
#
# --- Azure DNS ---
# apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
# kind: ClusterIssuer
# metadata:
#   name: letsencrypt-prod-dns
# spec:
#   acme:
#     server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
#     email: platform@example.com
#     privateKeySecretRef:
#       name: letsencrypt-prod-dns-key
#     solvers:
#       - dns01:
#           azureDNS:
#             subscriptionID: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000  # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             resourceGroupName: dns-rg                              # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             hostedZoneName: example.com                           # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             environment: AzurePublicCloud
#             managedIdentity:
#               clientID: 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000      # <-- CHANGE THIS (workload identity)
#
# --- Cloud DNS (GCP) ---
# apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
# kind: ClusterIssuer
# metadata:
#   name: letsencrypt-prod-dns
# spec:
#   acme:
#     server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
#     email: platform@example.com
#     privateKeySecretRef:
#       name: letsencrypt-prod-dns-key
#     solvers:
#       - dns01:
#           cloudDNS:
#             project: my-gcp-project         # <-- CHANGE THIS
#             serviceAccountSecretRef:
#               name: clouddns-sa-key         # <-- CHANGE THIS: k8s secret holding SA JSON key
#               key: key.json

---
# ── 4. Certificate — explicit (optional, Ingress annotation is simpler) ───
# When you need full control over the Certificate resource, define it
# explicitly instead of relying on cert-manager's ingress-shim.
# Most teams just use the annotation on the Ingress and skip this.
#
# apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
# kind: Certificate
# metadata:
#   name: app-tls
#   namespace: default               # <-- CHANGE THIS: must match the Ingress namespace
# spec:
#   secretName: app-tls              # must match Ingress tls[].secretName
#   duration: 2160h                  # 90 days (Let's Encrypt default)
#   renewBefore: 360h                # renew 15 days before expiry
#   issuerRef:
#     name: letsencrypt-prod
#     kind: ClusterIssuer
#   dnsNames:
#     - app.example.com              # <-- CHANGE THIS
#     - "*.app.example.com"          # wildcard — requires DNS-01 issuer above

---
# ── 5. Ingress reference reminder ────────────────────────────────────────
# Your Ingress (cd/kubernetes/_base/ingress.yaml) already has:
#
#   annotations:
#     cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
#   spec:
#     tls:
#       - hosts: [app.example.com]
#         secretName: app-tls
#
# That is all cert-manager needs to issue and renew the certificate.
# cert-manager watches for Ingress resources with this annotation and
# creates a Certificate object automatically (ingress-shim).
